core: SQL stands for Structured Query Language and is a standard language for accessing and manipulating databases (W3Schools); it is a domain-specific language for managing data, especially in a relational database management system (Wikipedia)
Pronunciation: 'sequel' (the historical pronunciation, from IBM's SEQUEL) or 'S-Q-L' spelled out (Oracle History of SQL; Wikipedia)

What SQL does: four core data operations — retrieve/query data, insert records, update records, delete records (W3Schools); Oracle's SQL Standards lists querying data and inserting, updating, and deleting rows among SQL's tasks

The two families: queries that read data versus commands that change it — the read/write split; SELECT is the read command and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE change data (W3Schools; each command has its own sibling lesson)

SQL is declarative: you describe what you want (a condition), and the database retrieves all matching rows in a single step without row-by-row navigation (Oracle); original example — ask for all customers in Portland, not the steps to walk the table

SQL is standard but varies: ANSI standard 1986, ISO standard 1987 (W3Schools), current standard ISO/IEC 9075 (Wikipedia); compliant products support the major commands in a similar manner but add proprietary extensions (W3Schools); Microsoft SQL Server communicates in its own dialect, Transact-SQL (Microsoft Learn)
Why SQL matters: Oracle calls SQL the common language for all relational databases — all major database management systems support it, so skills transfer between databases

Honest framing: SQL looks simple and gets deep, but the basics are learnable — an interpretive framing built on the standard's design of a small core of commands extended by clauses and vendor additions
supporting: History: SQL began at IBM as SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language), developed to use Codd's relational model; the first commercial SQL implementation was released in 1979 (Oracle History of SQL)
SQL does more than the four data operations: creating databases, tables, views, stored procedures, and setting permissions (W3Schools) — beyond this lesson's scope

The relational context: SQL works with relational databases, where data is stored in tables — each table is a named collection of rows, each row has the same set of named columns (PostgreSQL tutorial)
SQL works at the logical level: it processes sets of data as groups rather than as individual units (Oracle SQL Standards)
outOfScope: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE mechanics (sibling topics: databases-and-sql:foundations:insert, :update, :delete)
ORDER BY, LIMIT, joins, aggregate functions, GROUP BY, indexes, transactions (sibling topics)
SQL syntax in depth: only short illustrative queries (six lines or fewer) appear in this lesson
Vendor-specific features and dialect comparison in depth; no vendor recommendations

claims.claim: SQL stands for Structured Query Language and is a standard language for accessing and manipulating databases; it is a domain-specific language used to manage data, especially in a relational database management system.

SQL began at IBM as SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language), developed to use Codd's relational model; SEQUEL later became SQL and is still pronounced 'sequel', and the language is also pronounced by spelling it out, 'S-Q-L'. The first commercial SQL implementation was released in 1979.

SQL became a standard of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) in 1986 and of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in 1987; both ANSI and ISO/IEC have accepted SQL as the standard language for relational databases, and the current standard is published as ISO/IEC 9075.

SQL's core data operations are four: retrieve (query) data, insert records, update records, and delete records; Oracle's SQL documentation likewise lists querying data and inserting, updating, and deleting rows among SQL's tasks.

SQL statements divide into two families: queries that read data and commands that change it; W3Schools lists retrieving data separately from inserting, updating, and deleting records, and the individual commands (select, insert, update, delete) each have their own lesson in this course.

SQL is declarative: to retrieve a set of rows you define a condition that filters the rows, and all rows satisfying the condition are retrieved in a single step — you need not deal with the rows one by one; asking for 'all customers in Portland' states the what and leaves the how to the database.

SQL is standardized but varies between products: although SQL is an ANSI/ISO standard, there are different versions of the language; to be compliant, database programs support the major commands in a similar manner, but most also have their own proprietary extensions — for example, Microsoft SQL Server communicates using Transact-SQL (T-SQL).
SQL is the common language for all relational databases: all major relational database management systems support SQL, so SQL skills transfer from one database to another.

SQL works with relational databases, where data is stored in tables: each table is a named collection of rows, each row of a given table has the same set of named columns, and each column is of a specific data type.

Honest framing: SQL's core commands look simple and the language grows deep quickly, but the basics — reading, adding, changing, and removing data — are learnable; this interpretive framing rests on the standard's design of a small core of commands extended by clauses and vendor additions.

positions: Oracle's History of SQL states that SEQUEL later became SQL and is still pronounced 'sequel'.
Wikipedia and common usage record both pronunciations: 'S-Q-L' (spelled out) and 'sequel'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both: 'sequel' is the historical pronunciation carried over from SEQUEL, and 'S-Q-L' is the spelled-out form; either is acceptable in practice.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is SQL exactly the same in every database product?
positions: W3Schools notes that although SQL is an ANSI/ISO standard, there are different versions of the language, and most database programs have their own proprietary extensions.
Oracle states that all major relational database management systems support SQL, so skills transfer from one database to another.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The two statements are consistent: the standard defines a common core (the major commands behave similarly everywhere), while dialects and extensions account for the differences. The lesson teaches the standard core and notes the variation without favoring any vendor.
